rows: Listeria monocytogenes contamination can require withdrawal or recall of affected food.
Ready-to-eat foods can present particular Listeria control challenges.
Some people are more vulnerable to severe listeriosis.
Businesses should identify affected products using exact batch and date information.
Consumers should follow the action in the specific official recall notice.
Temperature, shelf life and environmental hygiene are important control factors.
Cleaning and environmental monitoring can support control in relevant facilities.
Incidents should trigger traceability, investigation and corrective action.
A product type or positive environmental sample does not prove that every unit is contaminated.
Batch conclusions require product, date, lot, sampling, distribution, storage and current recall evidence.
Food crime involves serious fraud and related criminality in food, drink or feed supply chains.
Food crime can affect safety, authenticity and consumer confidence.
Businesses should consider vulnerabilities in ingredients, suppliers and distribution.
Traceability and supplier assurance can help detect suspicious activity.
Adulteration, substitution and document fraud are recognised food-crime methods.
Suspected food crime can be reported confidentially to the National Food Crime Unit.
Poor hygiene without deliberate deception is generally handled through food-safety authorities rather than as food crime.
Businesses should investigate anomalies and preserve relevant evidence.
A price anomaly, origin claim or documentation error does not prove deliberate food crime.
Attribution requires product, supplier, transaction, laboratory, document, intent and investigative evidence.
